intro_text:
Sunnyside North Beach is a clothes-optional beach on Port Phillip Bay, about 12 kilometres from Frankston and south of Mount Eliza, Victoria. It is the only clothes-optional beach on the east side of the bay and one of just three legally designated clothing-optional beaches in the state, alongside Point Impossible near Torquay and Southside near Point Addis. The beach immediately next to the Sunnyside Road carpark is not the legal nude section — the designated stretch begins about 500 metres further along, reached via a dirt path through scrub or a walk along the beach itself over a rocky section.

The beach has carried its clothing-optional status since 1986. In November 2021, Mornington Peninsula Shire voted unanimously to ask the state planning minister to review that status — not the shire's first attempt; a review was floated in 2006 and went nowhere. In February 2022 a council report alleged regular drug use, sexual activity and syringes left in the carpark and surrounding bluffs, and revocation looked live. A community consultation drew almost 4,000 submissions, about 92% of them in favour of keeping the beach as it was, and on 6 December 2022 the council voted to retain the status.

Alongside that vote, council also sought state funding for police monitoring, camera surveillance, signage, carpark bays and access repairs. By October 2023, regulars reported none of it visible: the track down to the beach was still poorly kept, and an outdated warning sign was still sitting on the rocks. Paid parking had, by then, arrived at the carpark. The beach itself is sandstone rock, reef and bluff, with a rocky north end and a short sandy stretch; there is no lifesaver patrol, and the general hazard rating is 3 out of 10, among the least hazardous in the state.

Next to the beach sits the Morning Star Estate, a mansion built for London merchant Francis Alfred Gillett after he bought the land in 1865, later a Catholic boys' home that closed in 1975, and now a relisted heritage property — a genteel, unrelated identity sharing the same stretch of coast. Nothing in the public record used for this page confirms whether the promised safety upgrades, or the beach's status, changed after October 2023; that is where the available trail ends.
spike_explainer:
Sunnyside North Beach is Melbourne's only legal nudist beach, and for a year in 2021 and 2022 it was also nearly not one anymore. The status itself dates to 1986, granted under the Nudity (Prescribed Areas) Act 1983, a law that lets the state planning minister prescribe or revoke a clothing-optional area after consulting the local council. That mechanism is not abstract. Southside Beach, one of the only other two legally clothing-optional beaches in Victoria, exists today because a previous nude beach nearby had its status revoked outright — the real-world version of the outcome Sunnyside's regulars spent a year fighting.

**The council had tried before.** Mornington Peninsula Shire, or its predecessor, opposed the original 1986 gazettal and floated a review as early as 2006. Nothing came of it then, and the clothing-optional status stayed in place for another fifteen years. On 1 November 2021, the shire tried again, voting unanimously to write to the state planning minister seeking a formal review and public consultation into the beach's status. It was a procedural request, not a revocation, but it opened the door.

**What forced the issue was a council report, not a court case.** In February 2022, a report to council alleged that the carpark and the bluffs around the beach regularly saw drug use, sexual activity and syringes left behind as rubbish, at all hours of the day and night. That is a serious allegation, and it landed at exactly the moment the shire had already asked for a review. Longtime users of the beach did not deny the carpark had problems. Their argument was about geography: the drugs and the rubbish were happening in the carpark and the surrounding scrub, they said, not on the sand where clothing-optional status actually applied. It is a distinction that matters enormously to a legal designation and barely at all to a council trying to manage complaints about a public space.

**The response was public, fast, and lopsided.** A Facebook group organizing to keep the beach open passed 870 followers within months. A change.org petition gathered almost 800 signatures by May 2022, and by December it had grown past 1,800. A separate petition on a different platform, gopetition.com, sat at just 11 signatures in the same window — a reminder that petition counts vary wildly by platform and say less about total support than the platform that hosts them. What actually decided the outcome was the shire's own formal consultation, which the mayor described as possibly the largest community consultation the council had ever run: almost 4,000 submissions, with about 92% of respondents in favour of keeping the clothing-optional status as it was.

**On 6 December 2022, the council voted to retain the status.** For a campaign that had spent over a year bracing for revocation, it was, in the words of the man who led it, an emotional moment. But the same meeting that saved the beach's legal status also passed a second motion, seeking state government funding for the things the February 2022 report had actually complained about: police monitoring, surveillance cameras, carpark bays, signage, toilets, and repairs to the access track. That was the part meant to fix the underlying problem rather than just settle the legal question.

**Nearly a year later, none of it had shown up.** By October 2023, the same access track from the carpark to the clothing-optional stretch was reported to be in the same poor condition, with an outdated warning sign still sitting on the rocks despite the council having been told about it. A regular beachgoer, asked whether he'd seen any progress on the cameras, signage or carpark improvements, said there was no evidence of any of it — though he allowed that it might still be sitting somewhere in the shire's planning pipeline. What had changed, concretely, was that paid parking arrived at the carpark that same year. The council found the political win it needed. The infrastructure that was supposed to come with it did not, at least not by the last date this record covers.

The honest summary is that Sunnyside North Beach survived a genuine threat to a nearly four-decade-old legal status, on the strength of one of the largest community consultations the shire says it has ever run. What it has not visibly survived is the specific set of complaints — drugs, syringes, an unmaintained access track — that put its status at risk in the first place. Those were named as carpark and bushland problems, not beach problems, by the people defending the beach. As of the last reporting available, they were still just problems.
honest_reckoning_note:
The uncomfortable part of this story is not the nudity — it is that winning the political fight did not fix the thing that started it. Sunnyside North's clothing-optional status survived because almost 4,000 people told the council to keep it, at a roughly 92% margin, which is about as decisive a mandate as a local consultation produces. But the council's own December 2022 report acknowledged that drug use, sexual activity and syringes were a real problem at the carpark and surrounding bushland — and the motion it passed alongside the status vote, seeking funding for cameras, signage, police monitoring and access repairs, was the part meant to address that. Almost a year later, regulars said none of it was visible, and the track down to the beach was in the same condition that had helped trigger the review in the first place.

This page cannot tell you whether that changed later, because no source available for it covers anything after October 2023. What it can say is that a legal status was defended more successfully than the physical space around it was repaired, and that the gap between those two outcomes was still open at the last point anyone here checked.
reckoning_pullquote: The vote to keep the beach was almost unanimous in spirit; the follow-through on the safety complaints that caused the vote was not.

margin_notes.text: Do not confuse this with Southside Beach near Point Addis, 176 km away — a similarly named beach that itself replaced a nude beach whose legal status had been revoked, the real precedent for what a 'no' from the minister looks like.

The clothing-optional status exists because the Nudity (Prescribed Areas) Act 1983 lets the state planning minister prescribe or revoke such an area after consulting the council — the exact lever both the 2006 and 2021 review pushes tried to pull.
Regional sand modelling reads this stretch as a mixed quartz-feldspar-lithic regime, consistent with the sandstone bluffs and reef that dominate the shoreline rather than a pure sand beach.

The estate has its own separate market drama: listed for sale at $30 million in 2017, then relisted at $40 million by 2020 — a purely commercial identity crisis playing out beside the beach's political one.

day_in_time.dawn: At first light the carpark is empty and the walk to the clothing-optional stretch — about 500 metres along a dirt path or a rocky beach walk — is quiet; there is no lifesaver patrol at any hour.
day_in_time.midday: By midday, conditions are mixed but generally swimmable rather than rough; sandstone reef and bluff dominate the shoreline more than open sand.
day_in_time.golden: Toward evening, the free electric barbecues at the far end of the carpark are the closest thing to catering the beach offers — there is no food service on the sand itself.
day_in_time.night: After dark, the same carpark and bushland a 2022 council report flagged for drug use and syringes are unsupervised and unlit; the beach itself is not patrolled at any hour.

food_drink.description: There are no food stalls or kiosks at Sunnyside North Beach itself; the carpark has toilets, showers and free electric barbecues but no food service.

food_drink.description: Mount Eliza is the nearest township; no specific restaurant or cafe serving beach visitors is confirmed in the record used for this page.

food_drink.name: Bring your own
food_drink.description: Visitors typically bring their own food and water, using the free barbecues at the carpark's far end rather than buying food nearby.

access_note: Sunnyside North Beach is reached from a carpark at the end of Sunnyside Road, Mount Eliza, about 12 km from Frankston. The legal clothing-optional section is not the beach beside the carpark; it starts about 500 metres further along, via a dirt path through scrub or a walk along the beach over a rocky section. Paid parking applies at the carpark, 8am-8pm; Melbourne Moorabbin (MBW) is the nearest airport with published distance data.
